head: claude/mi94-register-id-uniqueness
title: MI-94: enforce register id uniqueness, and fix the session-key collision with a CHECK
body:
**MI-94**, parent `WO-20260903-THE-MONOLITHIC-REGISTERS-COLLIDE-ON-EVERY-SIBLING`, registry key `pending-20260903T073110Z`. Session `session_0174hCi1hhGzUKbtmL4jb8Rc`. Manager `session_01Nopk1HcpvWBSEbZxEmALkd`. START posted: [#6927 comment](https://github.com/benbaichmankass/Metis-Insights/issues/6927#issuecomment-5522278236).

**🛑 `landing: "hold"`, `hold_reason: changes_landing_machinery` — this needs ONE read from you, and the tier is not the objection.** `pr-landing-guard` R12 counts `scripts/ops/session_registry.py` as landing machinery (it generates the spawn prompt that tells every sub-session how to declare its tier and arm auto-merge). My edits there are register-side and touch no line of that prompt, but R12's reasoning holds anyway, so I did not arm auto-merge.

---

## 0 · I did not build what I was asked to build, and this is why

My brief said the obvious shape is one-file-per-row *"but argue the design from the constraints below rather than assuming that answer."* Arguing it says **don't**, and this repo has already measured why.

`docs/claude/work/README.md` and MI-76's PR body measured adjacent register-touching commit pairs and found the dominant conflict mechanism is the shared `updated_at`/`as_of` **header scalar**, not the rows — MANAGER-CHECKLIST **29/39 (74%)**, OPEN-PRS **8/12 (67%)**, SESSIONS **14/23 (61%)**. Sharding leaves that exactly where it is, because the scalar lives in the container. `.gitattributes` + `scripts/ops/merge_json_register.py` shipped instead, and `--check-round-trip` proves byte identity on all five registers.

So the storage shape is **not** the defect. I re-measured what is, on `main` @`855397f6`:

### Finding 1 — the remedy shipped and was armed in NO clone

`git config --get merge.jsonregister.driver` is **empty in a fresh clone**, and nothing in the `SessionStart` hook, any skill, or CI runs `scripts/ops/install_merge_driver.sh`. The only two references to it in the entire repo are a comment in `.gitattributes` and a code block in a README. Measured — two sibling branches each appending one row, then merged:

| | OPEN-ITEMS | MANAGER-CHECKLIST | SESSIONS | health-review-backlog |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| driver **not** armed | CONFLICT | CONFLICT | CONFLICT | CONFLICT |
| driver armed | *(n/a, below)* | **CLEAN** | **CLEAN** | **CLEAN** |

**4 of 4 without it.** That is your four hand-resolutions, reproduced. `manager_preflight.py` now FAILs an un-armed clone and names the one-line fix.

### Finding 2 — `registry_key` was duplicated on `main`, and `confirm()` mis-binds silently

Population = the 85 rows in `SESSIONS.json`. **14 carried a `registry_key`; only 12 were distinct.** `pending-20260902T133456Z` was shared by **three** rows — MI-66, MI-69, MI-70, all spawned in the same second.

`confirm()` took the **first** row matching a key and wrote to it. So confirming any one of those three would have bound that session's id onto **a different session's row**, silently — a mis-bind in the registry whose stated purpose is proving no sub-session was lost. That is worse than `BL-20260903-SESSIONS-REGISTRY-KEY-IS-SECOND-GRANULAR-AND-COLLIDES` describes.

### ⚠️ My own first experiment was invalid, and I caught it by checking my own output

My first sibling harness used the naive `json.dumps` writer and reported OPEN-ITEMS as a driver failure. It was **my harness** — that writer rewrites **2,082 of 1,065 lines** of `OPEN-ITEMS.json`, which is precisely the trap constraint 1 names. I walked into it inside my own instrument. Re-run through `backlog_append.append_row`, which is what a real session uses.

---

## 1 · The half git cannot do

A row-aware merge fixes the *textual* collision. It cannot see a **semantic** one: a branch files new work as `MI-86` while `MI-86` already exists as a different row. To git that is one changed value at one key — indistinguishable from *"we both edited this row"* — so the merge **deletes** what was there and reports success.

`scripts/ci/check_register_ids.py` — **`register-id-guard`**, `when: None`, every PR, over 10 register arrays:

| | catches | coverage |
|---|---|---|
| **R1** uniqueness | the branch **appended** a second `MI-86` | every row, every register |
| **R2a** creation-fact *and* headline both moved | a dated row re-filed under a live id | only rows recording a creation date — **31%** on MANAGER-CHECKLIST |
| **R2b** headline moved *and* under 25% of fields survived | the branch **replaced** `main`'s `MI-86` | every shared id, no date needed |
| **R3** a NEW row must record a creation date | the past grandfathered | makes R2a's number climb instead of sitting still |

### R2b is not redundant, and the incident proves it

I planted the real collision against the real `MI-86` on `main`, both spellings:

| spelling | before R2b | after |
|---|---|---|
| branch **appends** a second `MI-86` | **caught** (R1) | caught |
| branch **replaces** `main`'s `MI-86` | ⚠️ **rc=0 — walked straight through** | **caught** |

`main`'s `MI-86` carries no creation date, so R2a graded it `unassessable` and the guard missed the very incident that motivated it. R2b needs no date. It now prints what would have been destroyed:

> id `'MI-86'` was REPLACED, not edited — its headline changed (`'Night shift 2026-09-02→03 — handoff executed, lease released, brief due 05:00Z'` → `'a brand-new unrelated item filed blind'`) and only 17% of its fields survived … merging it DELETES `'Night shift …'`. Mint a fresh id.

A legitimate edit to that same row (state → `done`, note extended) still passes, rc=0.

### The 25% floor is MEASURED, not chosen by feel

**Population: 126,278 same-id row-pairs across adjacent commits** — OPEN-ITEMS 2,074 pairs / 84 commits · MANAGER-CHECKLIST 2,528 / 53 · health-review-backlog 121,676 / 120, from `git log --follow` as of 2026-09-03. Of those, exactly **16 changed a row's headline at all**, and the **lowest field-retention among those 16 real edits is 0.33**. A wholesale replacement retains ~0 by construction. The band between is wide and empty; 0.25 fires on **0 of 16**.

⚠️ **I corrected myself here.** My first measurement keyed on `title` alone and reported "headline changed: n=0", which would have justified a much blunter rule. Widening to the real headline field per register found 16, across 0.01%–0.6% by register. One measured corpus, not a law — if a legitimate rewrite ever trips it, change the constant and its measurement, not the guard's reach.

### Coverage is printed per register and never collapsed

A row with no creation date grades **`unassessable` — *we did not look*** — counted separately from passed. The guard's own output on `main`:

```
OPEN-ITEMS         items[id]             R2a  50/50   (100%)   R2b 100%
SESSIONS           sessions[session_id]  R2a  85/85   (100%)   R2b 100%
health-review      items[id]             R2a 1072/1149 (93%)   R2b 100%
MANAGER-CHECKLIST  items[id]             R2a   26/84   (31%)   R2b 100%  <- weakest, and where the incident was
OPEN-PRS           open_prs[pr]          R2a    0/2     (0%)   R2b 100%  <- no row carries a creation date
```

Reporting `MANAGER-CHECKLIST 31%` or `OPEN-PRS 0%` as a pass would be the *"green is not evidence"* shape. R1 and R2b cover them in full regardless.

## 2 · A finer clock is not the fix

`session_registry.py` minted `registry_key` from a second-granular timestamp with nothing looking at what was already there. **Microseconds only narrow the window** — and make the failure rarer and just as silent, which is worse. Uniqueness is a property of the set, so it is checked against the set:

- `_mint_registry_key` disambiguates against existing keys; a caller-**supplied** key that is taken is **refused**, never silently renamed (they named a specific row).
- `_refuse_duplicate_session_id` refuses re-registering a live id.
- **`confirm()` REFUSES an ambiguous key** and writes nothing, rather than binding the first match. A wrong binding reads as a complete record; refusing does not.

29 self-test controls pass, in both directions. Every mint case pins the **same** timestamp deliberately — a test that varied the clock would pass against the broken code too, which is exactly how this survived.

## 3 · The data repair — lossless, and proved

`SESSIONS.json` is byte-reproducible at `indent=2, ensure_ascii=False` (verified before writing). Assertions inside the transform, not after:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| rows | 85 | **85** |
| `session_id` values | 85 distinct | **85, identical list** |
| `registry_key` present / distinct | 14 / **12** | 14 / **14** |
| rows modified | — | **2** (exactly the 2 repaired) |
| diff | — | **6 insertions / 4 deletions** |

`pending-20260902T133456Z` becomes `-2` / `-3`, preserving the original mint second in the prefix and in `spawned_at`, with a `registry_key_repaired` note on each. Nothing was rewritten from scratch.

## 4 · The constraints, each verified rather than asserted

1. **`OPEN-ITEMS.json` never `json.load`/`json.dump` round-tripped** — I did not modify it at all.
2. **`backlog_append`'s duplicate-detection survives** — exercised both halves: an exact id repeat is refused, a restatement of an existing row raises `SimilarRowExists`, a novel row appends, and that append moves **10 lines, not 31,654**.
3. **The brief renderer still works** — `render_session_brief.py` gives `session-brief: OK — CLAUDE.md matches the registers`; `check_open_items.py` gives `OK — 50 items (33 monitoring)`, self-test PASS.
4. **Id-uniqueness enforced, and the key fixed with a CHECK** — above.
5. **Migration lossless and provable** — above. I read what existed before writing anything (`scripts/ci/check_test_schema_fidelity.py`, 2026-08-26).

## 5 · End to end

Two siblings each append a row through the real helper, merge with the driver, then the guard runs on the result: **MERGE CLEAN · 1,151 rows · 1,151 distinct ids · both probe rows survived · `register-id-guard: OK`.**

## 6 · Guards

`python3 scripts/ci/run_guards.py --base main` gives **PASS 84 · FAIL 0 · SKIP 0.**

`pytest` and `lint-imports` were absent from this container, so `layer-guard` and three pytest guards initially reported 127/1. **I installed both and re-ran rather than reporting them green** — the 84 above includes all four genuinely executing. `stated-population-guard` then caught a real defect **in my own PR** (a bare `35%` in the README); it now reads *23 of 65 adjacent commit pairs, against 8 of 91 (9%)*.

## 7 · Filed, not fixed — two things I found and left alone

- **`BL-20260903-OPEN-ITEMS-HAS-NO-APPEND-HELPER-AND-BACKLOG-APPEND-REFUSES-IT`** — `append_row` **cannot write `OPEN-ITEMS.json` at all**; none of its five candidate serialisations reproduces the file (the closest differ on 236 of 1,065 lines — it indents array *elements* one level shallower than `json.dumps` does at any setting). The refusal is correct, but it means the register with the **highest measured row contention (23 of 65 pairs, 35%)** is the one no tool can safely append to. Writing a serialiser for it is a separate, riskier change.
- **`BL-20260903-OPEN-PRS-ROWS-CARRY-NO-CREATION-DATE-SO-IDENTITY-CANNOT-BE-CHECKED`** — R2a covers 0% of its 27 rows. I did **not** back-fill dates; that would assert a fact nobody recorded, which the work-store README forbids for `asked_by` for the same reason.

## 8 · What this does NOT do, said plainly

- **It does not make a conflicted PR auto-mergeable on GitHub.** The merge driver is client-side; a `mergeable_state: dirty` PR is still dirty. What arming removes is the hand-resolution.
- **It does not remove the `as_of` contention at source.** MI-76 named that the highest-value change left, and it is a register-schema decision with a real consumer — `render_daily_brief.py` renders it as the register's freshness. I did not take it unasked. **On the measurement it is still the biggest remaining win, and it is yours to scope.**
- **R2b is one measured corpus.** 16 headline-changing edits is a small numerator.
- **The `merge_driver` check makes a clone report the gap; it does not install anything.** Wiring the installer into `SessionStart` touches session machinery and was outside my scope.
